# Exercise 5.4 — Random forests {#sec-random-forest}

A single decision tree is easy to read but unstable. A few different people in
the training rows can give a very different tree. A **random forest** grows
many trees and lets them vote. Two things make the trees differ from each
other:

- each tree is grown on a **bootstrap sample** of the training rows: as many
  rows as the training set, drawn at random with replacement;
- at each split, each tree may only try a **random subset of the predictors**.

The forest's prediction is the average of the trees' votes. The errors of the
single trees partly cancel out.

**Goal.** In this exercise you will:

- tune a random forest with a workflow and 5-fold cross-validation, as you did
  for the tree in Exercise 5.3;
- fit the final forest and evaluate it once on the test rows;
- compare it with your tuned tree.

:::::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

### Packages and data

```{r}
# Packages for this exercise. If one is missing, remove the # and run this line once:
# install.packages(c("tidyverse", "tidymodels", "ranger"))

library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)

theme_set(theme_bw())          # white background for every plot
options(pillar.sigfig = 3)     # show three significant figures in tables
```

The same 750 people and five predictors as Exercise 5.3, from
[`data/diabetes_clean.csv`](data/diabetes_clean.csv). The outcome has the levels
`neg` then `pos`.

```{r}
diabetes <- read_csv("data/diabetes_clean.csv") |>
  select(pregnant, glucose, mass, pedigree, age, diabetes) |>
  mutate(diabetes = factor(diabetes, levels = c("neg", "pos")))
```

The same split as before: 600 people for training and 150 for testing.

```{r}
set.seed(42)
split <- initial_split(diabetes, prop = 0.8)
train <- training(split)
test  <- testing(split)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Part 1 — From one tree to a forest

`rand_forest()` with the `ranger` engine. The number of trees is fixed at 500.
Two hyperparameters are marked with `tune()`:

- `mtry`: how many predictors each split may choose from (1 to 5 here);
- `min_n`: the smallest node that may still be split, as for the tree.

The model and the recipe go into a workflow, exactly as in Exercise 5.3. Only
the model line has changed.

```{r}
rf_spec <- rand_forest(mtry = tune(), min_n = tune(), trees = 500) |>
  set_engine("ranger") |>
  set_mode("classification")

rf_wf <- workflow() |>
  add_model(rf_spec) |>
  add_recipe(recipe(diabetes ~ ., data = train))
```

::: {.callout-important}
## Learning points
- A random forest is many trees, each grown on a bootstrap sample of the rows and trying a random subset of predictors at each split. Their votes are averaged.
- A small `mtry` makes the trees more different from each other.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Part 2 — Tuning `mtry` and `min_n`

Five values of each, 25 combinations. Each one is judged by 5-fold
cross-validation on the training rows, as in Exercise 5.3. That is 125 forests,
which takes a few seconds.

```{r}
rf_grid <- grid_regular(mtry(range = c(1L, 5L)),
                        min_n(range = c(2L, 10L)),
                        levels = 5)

set.seed(123)
folds <- vfold_cv(train, v = 5, strata = diabetes)

rf_res <- tune_grid(
  rf_wf,
  resamples = folds,
  grid      = rf_grid,
  metrics   = metric_set(roc_auc),
  control   = control_grid(event_level = "second")
)

autoplot(rf_res)
```

Now show the five best combinations by AUC:

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
show_best(rf_res, metric = ______, n = 5)
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
The metric is the one given to `metric_set()` above, written in quotes.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
show_best(rf_res, metric = "roc_auc", n = 5)
```

`mtry` 1 with `min_n` 8 has the best cross-validated AUC, 0.809. Next come 1
with 10 (0.807), 1 with 6 (0.805), 2 with 10 (0.805) and 2 with 6 (0.802). The
standard errors are about 0.015, so these five cannot really be told apart. In
the plot, a small `mtry` and a large `min_n` do best.
:::
:::

**Question!** Which values of `mtry` and `min_n` work best? Are the
differences large compared with the standard errors?

::: {.callout-important}
## Learning points
- Tuning a forest uses the same workflow, grid and folds as tuning a tree.
- Look at the whole grid, not only the winner: many combinations are close.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Part 3 — The final forest, evaluated once

Put the best combination into the workflow and fit it once on all 600 training
rows:

```{r}
best_rf <- select_best(rf_res, metric = "roc_auc")

set.seed(123)
final_rf_fit <- finalize_workflow(rf_wf, best_rf) |>
  fit(data = train)

test_preds <- predict(final_rf_fit, new_data = test, type = "prob") |>
  bind_cols(predict(final_rf_fit, new_data = test, type = "class")) |>
  bind_cols(test)
```

Now evaluate it on the test rows:

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
class_metrics <- metric_set(accuracy, sens, spec)
class_metrics(______, truth = diabetes, estimate = .pred_class,
              event_level = "second")
roc_auc(test_preds, truth = diabetes, ______, event_level = "second")
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
The predictions are in `test_preds`. The AUC needs the predicted probability of
`pos`, which is the column `.pred_pos`.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
class_metrics <- metric_set(accuracy, sens, spec)
class_metrics(test_preds, truth = diabetes, estimate = .pred_class,
              event_level = "second")
roc_auc(test_preds, truth = diabetes, .pred_pos, event_level = "second")
```

The forest uses `mtry` 1 and `min_n` 8. On the test rows: accuracy 0.733,
sensitivity 0.618, specificity 0.800, AUC 0.765.
:::
:::

**Question!** Look back at your tuned tree in Exercise 5.3. Is the forest
better on the test rows? Is it worth losing a single tree that you can read?

::: {.callout-important}
## Learning points
- Fit the final forest once on all the training rows, then use the test rows once.
- A forest is usually more accurate than a single tree, but it cannot be read as a picture.
:::

### Packages and data

```{python}
# Packages for this exercise. If one is missing, install it once from a terminal
# (in a Jupyter notebook, type %pip instead of pip):
# pip install pandas matplotlib scikit-learn

import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV, train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, recall_score, roc_auc_score
```

The same 750 people and five predictors as Exercise 5.3, from
[`data/diabetes_clean.csv`](data/diabetes_clean.csv). The outcome is 1 for `pos`
and 0 for `neg`.

```{python}
diabetes = pd.read_csv("data/diabetes_clean.csv")
diabetes = diabetes[["pregnant", "glucose", "mass", "pedigree", "age", "diabetes"]]
diabetes["diabetes"] = (diabetes["diabetes"] == "pos").astype(int)       # 1 = pos, 0 = neg

predictors = ["pregnant", "glucose", "mass", "pedigree", "age"]
```

The same split as before: 600 people for training and 150 for testing.

```{python}
train, test = train_test_split(diabetes, test_size=0.2, random_state=42)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Part 1 — From one tree to a forest

`RandomForestClassifier()` with 500 trees. `random_state` makes the forest the
same every time, and `n_jobs=-1` grows the trees on all the computer's cores.
Two hyperparameters will be tuned:

- `max_features`: how many predictors each split may choose from (1 to 5 here),
  called `mtry` in R;
- `min_samples_split`: the smallest node that may still be split, as for the
  tree.

Compared with Exercise 5.3, only the model line has changed.

```{python}
rf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=500, random_state=123, n_jobs=-1)
```

::: {.callout-important}
## Learning points
- A random forest is many trees, each grown on a bootstrap sample of the rows and trying a random subset of predictors at each split. Their votes are averaged.
- A small `max_features` makes the trees more different from each other.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Part 2 — Tuning `max_features` and `min_samples_split`

Five values of each, 25 combinations. Each one is judged by 5-fold
cross-validation on the training rows, as in Exercise 5.3. That is 125 forests.

```{python}
rf_grid = {"max_features":      [1, 2, 3, 4, 5],
           "min_samples_split": [2, 4, 6, 8, 10]}

rf_search = GridSearchCV(rf, param_grid=rf_grid, cv=5, scoring="roc_auc")
rf_search = rf_search.fit(train[predictors], train["diabetes"])

rf_results = pd.DataFrame(rf_search.cv_results_)
rf_results = rf_results[["param_max_features", "param_min_samples_split",
                         "mean_test_score", "std_test_score"]]

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for n in rf_grid["min_samples_split"]:
    rows = rf_results[rf_results["param_min_samples_split"] == n]
    ax.plot(rows["param_max_features"], rows["mean_test_score"], marker="o", label=str(n))
ax.set_xlabel("max_features (mtry)")
ax.set_ylabel("Mean cross-validated AUC")
ax.legend(title="min_samples_split")
plt.show()
```

Now show the five best combinations by AUC:

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
rf_results.sort_values(______, ascending=False).head(5).round(3)
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
Sort by the column that holds the mean cross-validated AUC, written in quotes.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
rf_results.sort_values("mean_test_score", ascending=False).head(5).round(3)
```

`max_features` 1 with `min_samples_split` 10 has the best cross-validated
AUC, 0.800. Next come 1 with 8 (0.800), 2 with 10 (0.799), 1 with 6 (0.797) and
2 with 8 (0.796). `std_test_score` is the spread across the five folds, about
0.033, so these five cannot really be told apart. In the plot, a small
`max_features` and a large `min_samples_split` do best.
:::
:::

**Question!** Which values of `max_features` and `min_samples_split` work
best? Are the differences large compared with the spread across folds?

::: {.callout-important}
## Learning points
- Tuning a forest uses the same pipeline, grid and folds as tuning a tree.
- Look at the whole grid, not only the winner: many combinations are close.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Part 3 — The final forest, evaluated once

`GridSearchCV()` has already refitted the best combination on all 600 training
rows:

```{python}
print(rf_search.best_params_)
final_rf = rf_search.best_estimator_

test_class = final_rf.predict(test[predictors])
test_prob  = final_rf.predict_proba(test[predictors])[:, 1]
```

Now evaluate it on the test rows. Sensitivity and specificity are as in
Exercise 4.3; in scikit-learn the specificity is the recall of class 0:

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
truth, predicted = test["diabetes"], ______
print("test accuracy:   ", round(accuracy_score(truth, predicted), 3))
print("test sensitivity:", round(recall_score(truth, predicted), 3))
print("test specificity:", round(recall_score(truth, predicted, pos_label=0), 3))
print("test AUC:        ", round(roc_auc_score(truth, ______), 3))
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
Accuracy, sensitivity and specificity need the predicted classes,
`test_class`. The AUC needs the predicted probabilities, `test_prob`.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
truth, predicted = test["diabetes"], test_class
print("test accuracy:   ", round(accuracy_score(truth, predicted), 3))
print("test sensitivity:", round(recall_score(truth, predicted), 3))
print("test specificity:", round(recall_score(truth, predicted, pos_label=0), 3))
print("test AUC:        ", round(roc_auc_score(truth, test_prob), 3))
```

The forest uses `max_features` 1 and `min_samples_split` 10. On the test
rows: accuracy 0.747, sensitivity 0.544, specificity 0.871, AUC 0.814.
:::
:::

**Question!** Look back at your tuned tree in Exercise 5.3. Is the forest
better on the test rows? Is it worth losing a single tree that you can read?

::: {.callout-important}
## Learning points
- Fit the final forest once on all the training rows, then use the test rows once.
- A forest is usually more accurate than a single tree, but it cannot be read as a picture.
:::

::::::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::: {.instructor}
**Teaching choice.** Cut to three parts: what a forest is, tuning with the same
workflow and 5-fold cross-validation as the tree, and one evaluation on the
test rows. The grid keeps the module lead's shape (five levels each); `mtry`
runs 1 to 5 because there are five predictors, `min_n` 2 to 10. In Python
`min_samples_split` mirrors ranger's `min.node.size`. The forest is compared
with the student's own tuned tree from Exercise 5.3.

**Expected values.** R (`set.seed(42)` split, `set.seed(123)`, ranger, 500
trees): best `mtry` 1, `min_n` 8, CV AUC 0.809 (SE 0.014); the whole grid lies
between 0.784 and 0.809. Test accuracy 0.733, sensitivity 0.618, specificity
0.800, AUC 0.765. Python (`random_state=42` split, `random_state=123`, 500
trees): best `max_features` 1, `min_samples_split` 10, CV AUC 0.800 (fold SD
0.032); the whole grid lies between 0.779 and 0.800. Test accuracy 0.747,
sensitivity 0.544, specificity 0.871, AUC 0.814. Students compare these with
their own tuned tree from Exercise 5.3. R and Python draw different random splits,
so their numbers differ.

**Common failures.** (1) `mtry` above the number of predictors: ranger stops
with an error, while scikit-learn silently uses all the predictors. (2)
Forgetting `set.seed()` before `fit()`, after which the R numbers move between
runs. (3) Setting `n_jobs=-1` on `GridSearchCV` rather than on the forest: the
search can stall when run through reticulate.

**Timing.** Tuning takes about 10 seconds in R and half a minute in Python. Part 1 ten
minutes, Part 2 fifteen, Part 3 fifteen.
:::
:::
